Populous
pŏp´ū-lŭs
adj. (full of people; numerous in inhabitants)
From the Latin populosus, from populus, a people. Scripture uses it twice: of what Israel became in Egypt, and of a great Egyptian city that fell anyway.

Biblical Definition

The confession an Israelite made when he brought his firstfruits begins with a wanderer and ends with a nation: “And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous” (Deuteronomy 26:5). The worshipper rehearses his own smallness before he presents his basket. The multiplication he describes was promised long before: “And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). The other use turns the same word into a warning. Nahum asks Nineveh to look at a city that had everything she has: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nahum 3:8). No — Thebes — was populous, moated, walled and defended, and it fell. Numbers are a blessing when God gives them and no defence when He does not: “There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength” (Psalm 33:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines populous as full of inhabitants; containing many inhabitants in proportion to the extent of the country.

expand to see more

POPULOUS, a. Full of inhabitants; containing many inhabitants in proportion to the extent of the country.

POPULATION, n. The whole number of people in a country, province, city or district.

MULTITUDE, n. The state of being many; a great number, collectively.

RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.

SOJOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 26:5 — "And thou shalt speak and say before the LORD thy God, A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous:"

Genesis 12:2 — "And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:"

Nahum 3:8 — "Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?"

Psalm 33:16 — "There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength."

Modern Corruption

Numbers are treated as the measure of a work's validity, which is precisely the confidence Nahum dismantles and the Psalms deny.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Scripture's double verdict on multitude. Israel's growth into a populous nation was a covenant blessing, explicitly promised to Abraham and explicitly confessed at the altar — so numbers are not despised. And populous No, with a river for a moat and the sea for a wall, was destroyed — so numbers are not trusted. The two statements sit in the same canon without tension because both are about who gives increase and who withholds deliverance.

The live misuse in the church is the use of attendance as the proof of faithfulness. It works in both directions and is wrong in both. A large congregation is taken as divine endorsement, and a small one as evidence of failure or of superior purity. Neither inference has any scriptural warrant. Gideon's army was reduced by God on purpose so that Israel could not vaunt itself; the crowd that followed our Lord for the loaves thinned to twelve when He preached hard words; and three thousand were added in a day at Pentecost. The confession an Israelite made over his basket keeps the right order: a perishing Syrian was my father, and God made him a nation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rab (H7227), many, numerous; goy gadol, a great nation; atsum (H6099), mighty; hamon (H1995), a multitude.

expand to see more

Hebrew rab (H7227) — many, great, populous; Deuteronomy 26:5.

Hebrew atsum (H6099) — mighty, numerous; great, mighty, and populous.

Hebrew goy (H1471) — a nation; what the sojourning few became.

Hebrew amon (H528) — populous, of the multitude; Nahum 3:8 of No.

Hebrew hamon (H1995) — a multitude, host; Psalm 33:16, no king saved by it.

Usage

"“Became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous” — the firstfruits confession."

"“Art thou better than populous No?” — a great city that fell."

"“No king saved by the multitude of an host” — what numbers cannot do."
